headline: New Zealand’s Election ‘Too Close to Call’ as Voters Turn to Minor Parties

paragraphs.text: New Zealand went to the polls on Saturday to decide who will lead the country at a moment of economic sluggishness and widespread political discontent. Preliminary results showed no clear front-runner, with many disgruntled voters choosing smaller parties over the major players.

Both Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s National Party, which is governing in a conservative coalition, and the main opposition, the center-left Labour Party, had been polling at near historic lows, signaling voters’ lack of faith in their ability to steer the nation out of its malaise.

Early results after polls closed at 7 p.m. local time showed the National Party neck and neck with Labour, both around 29.4 percent, with about 78 percent of the vote counted, according to the Electoral Commission.
Whichever party finishes first will almost certainly need to build a coalition to form a government under the country’s mixed-member, proportional electoral system.

The makeup will depend on the votes garnered by the libertarian ACT party and the populist New Zealand First on the right, and the Green Party and Maori Party on the left. A newly ascendant, centrist Opportunity Party is most likely to end up playing the role of kingmaker after clearing the 5 percent threshold to enter Parliament for the first time.

All votes are counted by hand, and the official result will not be released until Nov. 27. Negotiations for the formation of a government could take days or weeks, and may even stretch into the new year.
Here is what to watch for:
Cost of Living Worries

The victors will have a daunting task to turn around a dire economic picture that has many New Zealanders feeling bleak about their outlook and increasingly viewing moving overseas as the only option for making a decent living.

A surging cost of living is a leading concern, with four in 10 New Zealanders saying in a recent survey by the University of Otago that they were struggling to pay for essentials. Unemployment has edged up to 5.7 percent, the highest level since 2013. The country saw nearly 40,000 more citizens moving away than returning annually over the past two years.
Mr. Luxon and the National Party have sought to persuade voters to give them another chance at tackling inflation and government debt.
Chris Hipkins, who has led the Labour Party since Jacinda Ardern’s resignation in 2023, has centered his messaging on commitments to bring down health care and transportation costs.
Both parties were polling under 30 percent across multiple surveys leading up to the election.

“What we have seen from the two Chrises is a distinct lack of leadership, charisma and hope,” said Shamubeel Eaqub, the chief economist at Simplicity, a New Zealand fund management company. “This election, I think, will be remarked upon as one that was unsettling for its lack of vision and lack of hope at a time when people were really looking for it.”
Minor Parties, Major Roles
Lackluster support for the two major players has meant increased backing for the minor parties, each with its own priorities, personalities and political strategies.

All but one of the governments formed since the country adopted its current system in 1996 have been a coalition. Even so, the smaller parties will most likely play a larger role this time, with polls indicating that many will take a larger share of votes as people look for alternatives.

One contender that has emerged as a possible kingmaker is the Opportunity Party, headed by Qiulae Wong, a Fiji-born 38-year-old former business consultant. She has said Opportunity would be willing to work with either of the major parties to form a government.

Shortly after polls closed, Ms. Wong said it was “looking very likely” that the party could “make history tonight.” If Opportunity can hold its current share of the party vote, 5.8 percent, it will enter Parliament for the first time after contesting three elections.
“You guys have voted for unity over division,” Ms. Wong told a room of cheering and clapping supporters. “You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good.”

New Zealand First, which is led by the firebrand Winston Peters and has pledged to curb immigration, and the environmental Green Party have also seen their support increase. Voters in New Zealand cast ballots for both a local representative in Parliament and a party.
‘Division and Toxicity’

With bread-and-butter issues dominating, foreign policy has hardly figured into the race. New Zealand has to balance its heavy trade dependence on China while wrestling with the country, making its military heft increasingly felt in the region.
The National Party was voted into power in 2023 vowing to solidify relationships with the country’s traditional partners, the United States and Australia, and increase defense spending.
Asked in the final debate about managing relations with the United States, Kieran McAnulty, Labour’s campaign chair, said his party would approach the Trump administration differently.
“We saw yesterday with the results in the U.S. that the American people wholeheartedly rejected the division and the toxicity that we’re seeing in their politics over there,” he said on Thursday.
